issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may not disturb a statutory valuation tribunal’s land-compensation assessment without a qualifying error in principle, treatment of material evidence, or procedure.
material_facts: A statutory tribunal assessed the value of a large tract using comparable land values, an overall rise in local land prices, and an additional allowance for amenities associated with nearby improvement schemes.
Evidence supported the tribunal’s finding that the improvement schemes gave the relevant land benefits beyond the general rise in land prices.
The High Court removed the additional allowance, although the tribunal’s valuation was not shown to involve a qualifying error or procedural defect.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in interfering with the tribunal’s valuation, and the tribunal’s award was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Section 77A of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911, confined an appeal from the Tribunal to specified grounds, including a decision contrary to law, failure to determine a material issue of law, or a substantial procedural error possibly affecting the merits. A valuation tribunal’s factual findings could not be displaced merely because an appellate court preferred a different assessment; interference required an error of principle, disregard or misconstruction of important evidence substantially affecting valuation, or a substantial procedural defect. The Tribunal could account for the distinct effect of improvement schemes where evidence supported it; appreciation in localities benefiting from schemes could not be assumed to match appreciation elsewhere.

rule.if: land_acquisition_appeal and statutory_valuation_tribunal and valuation_supported_by_evidence and not material_error_of_principle and not material_evidence_misconceived and not substantial_procedural_defect

predicates.land_acquisition_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.statutory_valuation_tribunal: A tribunal established by law made the valuation under review.
predicates.valuation_supported_by_evidence: The tribunal’s valuation and its relevant adjustments were supported by evidence in the record.
predicates.material_error_of_principle: The tribunal applied an erroneous principle that materially affected its valuation.
predicates.material_evidence_misconceived: The tribunal ignored or misconstrued important evidence that substantially affected its valuation.
predicates.substantial_procedural_defect: A substantial procedural defect occurred that may have affected the merits of the valuation.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a statutory valuation tribunal’s evidence-supported land-compensation assessment and no material error of principle, misapprehension of important evidence, or substantial procedural defect is present, appellate interference with the valuation is unjustified.

issues.legal_issue: A compensation amount agreed between a claimant and an acquiring authority and accepted by the Collector may be evidence of the market value of land.
material_facts: The Collector’s order for other land recorded an agreed compensation figure reached by the claimant and the acquiring authority.
The Collector assessed other components of the property and accepted the agreed land value, although the Collector was not bound to accept the agreement.
The tribunal relied on that order in valuing adjacent land acquired at the same time.
issues.conclusion: The consent-based order had evidentiary value as evidence of market value, and the tribunal did not commit an error of law by relying on it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 11 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, the Collector performs a statutory duty and must exercise judgment in assessing compensation; the Collector is not controlled by an agreement between interested parties. As explained in Samiullah v. Collector of Aligarh, that duty remains the Collector’s. Nevertheless, a compensation agreement accepted by the Collector may be good evidence of market value, and an order based on such an agreement is not rendered devoid of evidentiary value merely because it was consensual. The tribunal’s reliance on such evidence did not furnish a ground for interference under Section 77A of the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911.

rule.if: land_compensation_valuation and collector_considered_the_property and formal_compensation_agreement_reached and collector_accepted_agreement

predicates.land_compensation_valuation: The proceeding requires the market value of land acquired for public purposes to be assessed.
predicates.collector_considered_the_property: The Collector considered the property or its relevant components when making the compensation order.
predicates.formal_compensation_agreement_reached: The claimant and acquiring authority formally agreed on compensation for the land.
predicates.collector_accepted_agreement: The Collector accepted the agreement and made an order on its basis, while remaining free not to accept it.

issues.definition: If, in a land-compensation valuation, the Collector considered the property and accepted a formal compensation agreement between the claimant and acquiring authority, the resulting consent-based order is relevant evidence of market value.

issues.legal_issue: The belting method is appropriate for valuing a large area of urban land where frontage land is more attractive than interior land.
material_facts: The acquired urban tract was large and had frontages on two roads as well as substantial interior land.
The tribunal divided the land into frontage and interior belts and applied lower per-unit values to belts farther from the roads.
The parties did not challenge the use of the belting method or the depth and relative valuation of the belts.
issues.conclusion: The belting method was appropriate for determining the market value of the large urban tract.
issues.legal_principle: Market value for compulsory acquisition is assessed under Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as modified by the Calcutta Improvement Act, 1911. Where a large area in an urban locality is acquired, the belting method is appropriate because land fronting main roads is ordinarily more attractive than land without such frontage.

predicates.large_urban_land_acquisition: A large area of land in an urban locality is being valued for acquisition.
predicates.land_has_road_frontage_and_interior_dept: The land includes frontage along roads and interior portions set back from those roads.

issues.definition: When a large urban tract being valued for acquisition includes both road-frontage land and interior land, the belting method is appropriate for its valuation.
